lesson.title: Reading Limits Straight Off the Curve
lesson.summary: A graph often reveals a limit's value, or its nonexistence, more directly than any algebra, once you know to trace the curve from both sides and watch for holes, jumps, and matching heights.
lesson.body:
Graphs give a second, visual route to the same limit ideas already built numerically and intuitively (prerequisites: intuitive limit and graphing functions). The technique is to trace along the curve from the left toward some x-value a, and separately trace from the right toward a, asking what height, what y-value, the curve seems to be heading toward, not what height the curve actually reaches at a itself, which might be a different value entirely or might not exist at all.

This gives the left-hand limit, written lim as x approaches a from the left, read from the part of the graph where x is less than a, and the right-hand limit, written lim as x approaches a from the right, read from the part where x is greater than a. The two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree on the same number; if the curve approaches different heights from the two sides, a visible jump, the two-sided limit does not exist, no matter how well-behaved the function is on either side individually.

Worked example, describing what such a graph shows: let f(x) = x + 1 for x less than 2, let f(2) = 5 (a single point plotted well away from the rest of the curve), and let f(x) = x^2 - 1 for x greater than 2. On a graph this looks like a line climbing toward an open circle at (2, 3), a separate solid dot plotted up at (2, 5), and a curve on the right also approaching that same open circle at (2, 3). Reading the left-hand limit: as x approaches 2 from the left, x + 1 approaches 3. Reading the right-hand limit: as x approaches 2 from the right, x^2 - 1 approaches 4 - 1 = 3. Both sides approach the same height, 3, so lim as x approaches 2 of f(x) equals 3, even though the graph shows f(2) actually equals 5. This is a removable discontinuity: a hole at height 3 with a stray point plotted elsewhere.

Contrast that with a jump discontinuity, visible on a step-shaped graph: f(x) = -1 for x less than 0, and f(x) = 1 for x greater than or equal to 0. Reading the graph, the left-hand limit as x approaches 0 is -1, and the right-hand limit as x approaches 0 is 1. These disagree, so lim as x approaches 0 of f(x) does not exist, even though f(0) = 1 is perfectly well defined. The two questions, does f(a) exist, and does the limit at a exist, are genuinely separate, and a graph makes that separation obvious in a way that a formula alone sometimes does not.

A graph can also show a third behavior: if the curve shoots upward or downward without any bound as x approaches a from one or both sides, the way 1/x behaves near x = 0, the limit is described as infinite rather than as a specific finite height. That case is developed fully in the infinite limit chapter, but it is worth recognizing on sight: a vertical asymptote on a graph is the visual signature of an infinite limit.

A practical reading habit: cover everything on one side of the target x-value with a hand or a sheet of paper, and watch only where the visible part of the curve is heading as it approaches that vertical line. Open circles mark a height the function approaches but does not actually take there, while solid dots mark the true, defined value of the function at that x.
